title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview
========
This playbook captures the canonical operational and engineering guidance for Redwood's serving runtime: high-level architecture, kernel scheduling and tunables, profiling and triage playbooks, benchmarking suite and methodology, release notes conventions, known issues and mitigations, and day-2 runbooks for on-call and SRE. It is intended for runtime engineers, performance-focused SREs, and platform owners.

Goals
-----
- Provide a single, discoverable reference for designing and operating the runtime with predictable latency and throughput.
- Standardize kernel and scheduler settings across cloud and private deployments.
- Define profiling and benchmarking procedures so regressions are reproducible and actionable.
- Codify release-note and roll-out steps for runtime changes that affect performance.

Audience and ownership
----------------------
- Primary: eng-serving-runtime (runtime engineering) — owner: Aisha Patel.
- Secondary: eng-sre, eng-infra, eng-platform, product (runtime-impacting features).
- On-call: runtime-sre rotation (see runbooks section).

1) Runtime architecture (summary)
--------------------------------
The runtime is split into four logical layers:
1. Front-door API layer (request validation, auth, routing)
2. Scheduling & routing layer (batching, model router, fallback policies)
3. Execution engine (kernels, attention optimizations, quantized execution)
4. Cache & KV layer (prefix caching, KV cache extraction and eviction)

Key principles:
- Single binary per target GPU family; configuration drives model variants, precision, and kernel selection.
- Continuous batching: requests are pooled with latency SLO awareness and dispatched to worker pools by objective function (latency vs throughput).
- Smart routing: policy-driven model selection with region/capacity fallbacks.
- Observability hooks at token, request, and model levels for cost attribution and quality checks.

SLOs and thresholds
-------------------
- P95 latency (request to first token): 120 ms for short-chat (<=64 tokens) on standard configs.
- P99 latency: 250 ms for short-chat.
- Throughput: normalized tokens/sec per GPU reported in benchmarking tables below.
- Error budget: 99.9% availability target per runtime process in Dedicated clusters.

-------------------

2) Kernel scheduling and OS tunables
------------------------------------
Overview:
The runtime relies on predictable kernel execution. Kernel scheduling here refers to both (a) which CUDA/cuDNN/cuBLAS kernels are selected at compile/runtime, and (b) OS-level scheduler and CPU affinity settings that affect host-to-device work dispatch. We recommend the following baseline across hosted and private deployments.

Baseline OS and cgroup settings
- cpuset: isolate CPU cores used by the runtime process and dedicate 1-2 cores for the host agent.
- cpu.shares: set to high priority for runtime processes to reduce throttling.
- memsw: disabled; avoid swapping.
- nohz_full: enable on cores dedicated to runtime where supported.

Recommended sysctl tunables (example values)
- vm.swappiness = 1
- net.core.somaxconn = 1024
- fs.file-max = 524288
- vm.max_map_count = 262144

Kernel scheduler and affinity rules
1. Pin the runtime main thread and IO threads to a dedicated cpuset (eg cores 2-7).
2. Use irqbalance pinned exceptions: ensure GPU interrupts are not migrated to runtime cores.
3. For multi-GPU hosts: localize host threads for each GPU to sibling CPU sets to reduce cross-socket latencies.

Tunable table (informational)
| Component                  | Key tunable / file                         | Recommended value            | Rationale |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------|------------------------------|-----------|
| Swap policy               | /proc/sys/vm/swappiness                    | 1                            | Minimize swapping
| Network backlog           | /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn               | 1024                         | Avoid connection drops under load
| Open files                | /proc/sys/fs/file-max                     | 524288                       | High fd usage from many connections
| mmap mappings             | /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count                | 262144                       | Large memory-mapped KV caches

Note: the table above is descriptive; exact values should be validated in benchmarking (see next section) and may vary for on-prem appliances.

Kernel selection guidance (runtime internals)
- The compilation pipeline emits multiple kernel variants per operator (small/medium/large batch shapes). At runtime the kernel picker chooses based on: sequence length, current batch size, model precision, and HW family.
- Fallback order: fast-approx -> numerically-safe -> vectorized-safe. Documented in kernel_manifest.json included in each release.

3) Profiling and triage playbook
--------------------------------
Goal: reproducibly collect traces and resource metrics when performance regressions are observed.

When to profile
- Latency/P95/P99 breaches observed in dashboards for 3+ minutes.
- New runtime release or kernel change rolled out (canary phase).
- Customer report of sluggish responses with sample request.

Quick triage checklist (ordered)
1. Verify service health and recent deploys (PagerDuty runbook -> check last deploy id).
2. Capture a live profile: use the runtime /debug/trace endpoint with profiling=cpu,gpu,kv for 30s.
3. Collect perf counters from host: nvidia-smi dmon, nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv -l 1 for 30s.
4. Collect OS-level counters: pidstat -urd 1 30, vmstat 1 30.
5. Dump runtime logs at DEBUG for the window; include batching stats and kernel selection logs.
6. Re-run synthetic benchmark (see benchmarking section) that matches the failing workload.
7. Create a triage ticket with artifacts and initial hypothesis.

Recommended commands (examples)
- Start a 30s runtime trace: curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:8080/debug/trace?profiling=cpu,gpu,kv&duration_s=30" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TRACE_TOKEN"
- GPU counters: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -lms 1000 -f /tmp/gpu-counters.csv &
- Host perf (Linux): sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 30; sudo perf script > /tmp/perf-script.out

What to collect in the ticket
- Dashboard links and alert window.
- Trace archive (trace.json / perf.data).
- Kernel selection log excerpt (kernel_manifest & chosen variants).
- Synthetic benchmark run id and results.
- Any recent config changes (kernel flags, cpuset changes).

4) Benchmarking suite and methodology
------------------------------------
Benchmarking goals:
- Produce stable, comparable token/sec and latency numbers across model families and hardware profiles.
- Validate impact of kernel changes, quantization, and batching heuristics.
- Provide reproducible artifacts for release notes.

Benchmark components
- harness/runner: orchestrates synthetic workloads and records traces.
- workload profiles: chat-short (<=64 tokens), chat-mid (65-512), completion-long (512-2048), embeddings-bulk (batch sizes 16..256).
- metrics collector: collects token/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, memory usage, kernel variant usage.

Standard benchmark procedure
1. Provision a host with stable background load (ideally isolated).
2. Warm-up: run 10 identical short-chat requests to populate KV cache.
3. Run each workload profile for N=300 samples (or 300s) and collect metrics.
4. Run each benchmark 3 times and report the median of medians.
5. Archive artifacts and assign run id (bench-<YYYYMMDD>-<tag>).

Example output format (JSON bytes as string)
{
  "run_id": "bench-20260304-runtime-kernel-test",
  "hardware": "A100-80GB",
  "model": "redwood-3b-q8",
  "workload": "chat-short",
  "p50_ms": "22.4",
  "p95_ms": "110.0",
  "p99_ms": "198.6",
  "tokens_per_sec": "7200"
}

Benchmarking acceptance criteria
- Any change that decreases tokens/sec by >7% for a given workload and hardware requires a pre-approved rollback plan and an incident postmortem if shipped.
- Any regression in P99 >20% must block the release for that target hardware.

5) Release notes and rollout checklist for runtime changes
--------------------------------------------------------
Required content for runtime release notes
- Brief summary of change (one sentence).
- Affected components (kernel picker, scheduler, batcher, runtime binary).
- Benchmark artifacts (run ids and links).
- Canary plan and rollout windows.
- Rollback instructions and known mitigations.

Rollout steps (recommended)
1. Developer e2e tests and local micro-benchmarks.
2. CI benchmarking gate: new change must run harness and meet acceptance criteria (see benchmarking section).
3. Canary (2-5% of traffic) for 24 hours with enhanced profiling on.
4. Progressive ramp: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 1 hour observation windows. Abort if P95 breaches 2x baseline or error rate increases >0.5%.
5. Post-rollout: publish detailed performance notes and link artifacts.

6) Known issues and mitigations (current)
---------------------------------------
- Issue: Occasional P99 spikes on chat-short when KV cache eviction occurs simultaneously with large batched requests.
  - Mitigation: Adjust eviction thresholds (cache.eviction_target = 0.85) and enable staggered cache trimming on high load.
- Issue: On some older NICs, high connection churn produces syscall stalls that increase latency by ~30ms.
  - Mitigation: increase net.core.somaxconn and enable accept filters on the front-door.
- Issue: CUDA/cuBLAS kernel hang observed with specific small-batch matrices on driver 530.x.
  - Mitigation: pin to 535.x for affected fleets and apply kernel-selection fallback (numerically-safe).

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)
--------------------------------------------
Runbook: High P99 latency
1. Acknowledge alert and capture initial dashboard snapshot.
2. Check recent deploys and canary status.
3. Run profiling playbook (see section 3).
4. If kernel hang suspected: scale down affected pool and route traffic to fallback model variant.
5. Notify customers per SLA if incident escalates.
6. Open incident ticket and follow incident-response template.

Runbook: Node GPU OOMs
1. Detect repeated OOMs from logs (GPU memory exceeded).
2. Quarantine node and stop runtime service.
3. Re-run diagnostic: capture dmesg, nvidia-smi, and runtime logs.
4. If caused by KV cache growth, reduce cache.max_entries by 25% and redeploy.
5. Reintegrate node after verification.

Runbook: Kernel regression detected in CI
1. Reproduce benchmark locally using the harness runner with the failing commit.
2. Bisect commit range and isolate kernel change.
3. Add a focused micro-benchmark for the affected operator.
4. If fix not immediate: revert to previous runtime binary for the affected hardware target.

8) Team wiki and knowledge sharing
----------------------------------
- Canonical artifacts are stored in the benchmarks bucket: s3://redwood-runtime-benchmarks/<run_id>/
- Kernel manifests and selection logs live in the release artifact: artifacts/runtime/<version>/kernel_manifest.json
- Weekly sync: runtime-team-weekly (agenda includes any perf regressions, outstanding known issues, and upcoming kernel changes).
- Training: quarterly cross-team perf review with eng-sre and customer-success to review field incidents.
